newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala peace talks could resume at weekend.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala peace talks could resume at weekend.

text.p: Peace talks between Guatemalan rebel guerrillas and the government could resume as early as this weekend and a final peace agreement is still on track to be signed in December, Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu said on Friday.
Guatemala's five-year-old peace process was interrupted Oct. 28 after a rebel commander was arrested for kidnapping a wealthy elderly woman for ransom.

After 12 days of tense government silence, and a series of olive branches offered by the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG in Spanish), both sides said on Thursday they were ready to return to negotiations.

"It will probably be Saturday or Sunday when we begin the negotiations again .... I am confident that we will be able to make up for lost time," Arzu said at a news conference before he flew to Chile to attend an Ibero-American Summit.

Arzu said it was up to the United Nations moderator, who observes the talks and acts as a go-between, to set the exact date for both sides to meet again in Mexico City, the traditional site of Guatemalan peace talks.

The president said peace negotiators would begin discussing a bilateral ceasefire instead of continuing talks about the post-war political role of the guerrillas, the topic on the table when talks were interrupted.

Guatemalans are anxious for the formal end of a 36-year-old armed conflict -- the last in Central America. More than 100,000 people, mostly civilians, have died in the war and an estimated 40,000 are missing.

The talks, which had been running smoothly for months, were abruptly suspended after rebel commander Rafael Valdizon was arrested on suspicion of kidnapping a woman belonging to the influential family that owns Guatemala's only cement company.

Police briefly jailed Valdizon but let him go in return for his freeing 86-year-old Olga Alvarado de Novella, whose whereabouts were still unknown to authorities. Police are searching for Valdizon, and Arzu promised he would be prosecuted if rearrested.
The URNG has often kidnapped people for ransom to finance its insurrection, but pledged to end such practices under preliminary agreements reached with the government.
After the government charged the guerrilla with violating terms of the negotiations and suspended talks, the URNG high command made a series of conciliatory gestures.
Firstly they condemned the kidnapping, and a few days later they announced they would suspend armed propaganda exercises by guerrillas in Guatemala.

But the government didn't respond until rebel commander Rodrigo Asturias (alias Commander Gaspar Ilom), Valdizon's direct leader within one of the four factions that make up the URNG, announced on Thursday he would withdraw from the talks.
